text: Welcome to This is My Architecture. My name is Peter. I'm here with Ryan from William Hill. Hi Ryan, good to have you here.
Thanks for having me.
Alright, so what do you guys do?
So William Hill is one of the world's leading betting and gaming companies. We provide gaming applications for customers all around the world on many different platforms.
Alright, I know that you've been subject to a larger DDoS attack some time ago and you've decided to move your security posture into the cloud. What's the actual issue you've had to deal with?

So in 2016 we were the victims of a major DDoS attack which utilized one of the largest botnets of the time, the Mirai botnet. And at its peak we were hit with over 177 gigabits a second which impacted our applications.
Alright, that's something. So you've chosen a couple of services. Let's talk through the architecture.
Sure, so in front of all of our applications we have CloudFront. And we use CloudFront's partner applications to mitigate against DDoS.
So we use Shield Advanced to be able to mitigate both layer 3 and layer 4 DDoS attempts. Things such as ACK floods or SYN floods. Also low complexity layer 7 attacks such as H2P floods.
For more complicated layer 7 attacks we use WAF where we can create filters to block more complicated attacks.
Alright, so use Shield Advanced to increase scale out to swallow the incoming flood and use WAF to make sure that you block. Now there's more to this. Talk us through.
Sure, so from CloudFront and the protection that's therein we send the traffic across to Route 53 where we have two separate Route 53 hosted zones.
One for traffic going to an ELB.

For traffic going to an ELB we just send non-sensitive traffic. But for more sensitive traffic we send the traffic across to an EC2 instance which hosts a F5 Big IP which is another form of WAF and that adds an extra layer of protection on top of the WAF we already have on CloudFront.
I see. So you do basically introduce another layer to make sure that you are able to tackle even more types of variations of attacks with F5 being involved here.
I see this is happening within a VPC. There's a segregation. What happens to the rest of the services?
Yeah, so once the traffic goes through the VPC we send it across to a VPC peering which sends the traffic to one of our seven different channel accounts where our applications actually are.
So from the VPC peering we see it goes across to the VPCs in those accounts which allows developers to create applications with the DDoS protection already built in.
I see. So you do send filtered and non-filtered traffic down here to your cloud environment and there's on-prem involved as well. I see Direct Connect. How does that collaborate?
Sure, yeah. So we're still in the process of migrating to the cloud so we have a number of applications that actually sit on our on-premise data centers.
So traffic from both EC2 instances and from the ELB go through to Direct Connect which then allows our customers traffic to go to our on-prem application servers.
All right. Okay. So we end with this part on-premise involved. But I see some more services. What about these?
Sure. Yeah. So for an added layer of protection we send traffic. We send logs of our traffic from CloudFront over to an S3 bucket.
From there we then send the logs across to our on-premise analysis servers which use both proprietary and third-party analytics and equations to be able to identify further malicious traffic.
Once that traffic is identified, we then send the IP addresses back up to AWS and to this DynamoDB instance we see here.
And there's a...basically the IP addresses are added to a table within DynamoDB, both with an expiration date due to the nature of IP addresses and them changing constantly.
There is a Lambda function which then runs that inspects that table for any new entries or for any expired entries.
And then updates the WAF filters with those IP addresses.
So it looks like a continuous improvement flow to your WAF filters.
Utilize the Direct Connect connection with low latency and high bandwidth to make sure that you have no losses in terms of...
...the WAF connection. And yeah. Thank you Ryan. Thanks for sharing this very interesting solution.
And thanks for watching. This is my architecture.
